topic.name: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Form Using Orthogonal Transformations

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-4x_1x_2+4x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-5\lambda &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 5, \, 0 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=-3x_1^2+2x_1x_2-3x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} -3-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2+6\lambda + 8 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= -2, \, -4 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=-2,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-2) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} - (-2) \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-4,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-4) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} - (-4) \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text:
\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=3, \quad$ $\lambda_2=2, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 3 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=2,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt 2,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0& -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1& 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text:
\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=2, \quad$ $\lambda_2=0, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=2,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=-2,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-2) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - (-2) \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt 2,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1& 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text:
\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=3, \quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 3 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=-1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-1) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - (-1) \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
